notes.front: What are the three pillars of observability in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Metrics, logs and traces.
notes.explanation: Control plane components and many add-ons emit all three; aggregating and correlating them shows the state, performance and health of the cluster.
notes.example: A latency spike: metrics show when it started, traces show which service was slow, logs show the error it hit.

notes.front: What is Prometheus, in one sentence?
notes.back: An open-source monitoring and alerting toolkit that collects and stores metrics as time series (values recorded with their timestamp).
notes.explanation: Kubernetes components expose metrics in Prometheus format, and a typical metrics pipeline scrapes them into a store such as Prometheus.
notes.example: A metrics pipeline periodically scrapes each kubelet’s `/metrics` endpoint and stores the samples in Prometheus.

notes.front: What are Prometheus metric types?
notes.back: Counter, gauge, histogram and summary: the four core kinds of metric that Prometheus client libraries offer.
notes.explanation: The type tells you how a value behaves, for example whether it can only go up. Each of the four has its own card.
notes.example: Requests served only ever rise (a counter); memory in use rises and falls (a gauge).

notes.front: What is OpenTelemetry, in one sentence?
notes.back: An open-source, vendor- and tool-agnostic framework and toolkit for generating, exporting and collecting telemetry such as traces, metrics and logs.
notes.explanation: It standardises how code is instrumented (instrumenting means adding the calls that emit telemetry), so you learn one set of APIs and keep ownership of your data, with no vendor lock-in.
notes.example: A service instrumented once with OpenTelemetry can send traces to Jaeger or to a commercial backend without re-instrumenting.

notes.front: What is OTLP?
notes.back: The OpenTelemetry Protocol, the standard protocol for telemetry data; Kubernetes components use it to export traces.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes components have built-in gRPC exporters for OTLP, so their spans (timed steps of a request) can go to a collector (a relay) or straight to a backend (the store you search).
notes.example: The kube-apiserver generates spans for incoming HTTP requests and exports them over OTLP to a collector.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Traces For Kubernetes System Components”

notes.front: What are cluster-level logging architectures?
notes.back: Designs for collecting container logs across a cluster, needed because Kubernetes has no native cluster-level logging.
notes.explanation: The options are a node-level logging agent, a sidecar container for logging, or the application pushing logs itself; each has its own card.
notes.example: A team wants to search the logs of all 200 Pods in one place, instead of running `kubectl logs` one Pod at a time.

notes.front: What is kube-state-metrics?
notes.back: An add-on agent that reads the Kubernetes API and exposes metrics about the state of objects, such as a Pod’s phase.
notes.explanation: It enriches the component metrics with object status, so Prometheus can query or alert on things like Pods that aren’t ready.
notes.example: An alert fires when a Pod has been stuck `Terminating` for more than 5 minutes, using kube-state-metrics data.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Metrics for Kubernetes Object States”

notes.front: What is cAdvisor?
notes.back: A daemon, included in the kubelet, that collects, aggregates and exposes container metrics, such as resource usage.
notes.explanation: It is the first link of the resource metrics pipeline that ends in the Metrics API.
notes.example: The CPU figure `kubectl top` shows for a Pod starts as a cAdvisor reading on that Pod’s node.

notes.front: As a pillar of observability, what is a metric?
notes.back: A numerical measurement, recorded over time as a time series.
notes.explanation: What you measure depends on the application: request times for a web server, active connections for a database.

notes.front: As a pillar of observability, what do logs provide?
notes.back: A chronological record of events inside applications, system components and security-related activity such as audit logging.
notes.explanation: In Kubernetes, container logs come from what applications write to stdout and stderr.

notes.front: As a pillar of observability, what do traces capture?
notes.back: How requests move across components and applications, linking the timing and relationships between operations.
notes.explanation: They let you see a request’s end-to-end flow and find bottlenecks.

notes.front: In what format, and at which endpoint, do Kubernetes components expose their metrics?
notes.back: In Prometheus format, at their `/metrics` endpoints.
notes.explanation: The kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, kube-proxy and kubelet all do this; a pipeline scrapes them into a time series database.

notes.front: Besides `/metrics`, which three metrics endpoints does the kubelet expose?
notes.back: `/metrics/cadvisor`, `/metrics/resource` and `/metrics/probes`.
notes.explanation: Add-ons such as kube-state-metrics enrich these signals with Kubernetes object status.

notes.front: Unlike the components’ `/metrics` endpoints, how is the Metrics API served?
notes.back: Through the Kubernetes API aggregation layer, by Metrics Server or another implementation.
notes.explanation: Your cluster must run Metrics Server or another implementation that provides the API.

notes.front: How do an application’s container logs reach `kubectl logs`?
notes.back: The container runtime captures its stdout and stderr, and the kubelet makes them available in the standard CRI logging format.
notes.explanation: Runtimes capture the streams in different ways, but the integration with the kubelet is standardised.

notes.front: Which node-level logging agents does the Kubernetes documentation give as examples?
notes.back: Fluent Bit and Fluentd.
notes.explanation: They tail the log files on each node and forward entries to a central log store.

notes.front: How is a node-level logging agent usually run, and why?
notes.back: As a DaemonSet, because it must run on every node.
notes.explanation: That gives one agent per node, and the applications on the node need no changes.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Logging Architecture”, “Using a node logging agent”

notes.front: What are the two drawbacks of running a logging agent in a sidecar container?
notes.back: It can use significant resources, and its logs can’t be read with `kubectl logs`, because the kubelet doesn’t control them.
notes.explanation: Use it only when a node-level agent isn’t flexible enough for the application.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Logging Architecture”, “Sidecar container with a logging agent”

notes.front: What does a streaming sidecar container do with application logs?
notes.back: Reads them from a file, a socket or journald, and prints them to its own stdout or stderr.
notes.explanation: The node’s kubelet and logging agent then handle them like any other container’s logs.

notes.front: Where do the kubelet and the container runtime write their own logs?
notes.back: To journald (the system log service) on machines with systemd; otherwise to `.log` files in `/var/log`.
notes.explanation: They run directly on the host, not in containers. System components that do run in containers always write to `/var/log`.

notes.front: How can Kubernetes components export trace spans?
notes.back: Over OTLP, either directly with their built-in gRPC exporters or through an OpenTelemetry Collector (a relay that processes telemetry).
notes.explanation: The Collector can sample or redact spans before sending them to a tracing backend.

notes.front: On which port do Kubernetes components export traces by default?
notes.back: 4317, the IANA-registered OpenTelemetry port, using the gRPC exporter for OTLP.
notes.explanation: A collector receiving Kubernetes traces therefore listens for OTLP over gRPC on 4317.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Traces For Kubernetes System Components”, “Trace Collection”

notes.front: What does the OpenTelemetry Collector do?
notes.back: Receives telemetry, processes it (for example by sampling or redaction) and exports it onward, such as to a tracing backend.
notes.explanation: The OpenTelemetry docs call it a proxy that receives, processes and exports telemetry data.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Observability”, “Traces”; OpenTelemetry documentation, “What is OpenTelemetry?”

notes.front: How does Prometheus store metrics?
notes.back: As time series: each value with the timestamp at which it was recorded, alongside optional key-value pairs called labels.
notes.explanation: Labels are what make Prometheus data multi-dimensional.

notes.front: In Prometheus’s data model, what identifies a time series?
notes.back: Its metric name plus a set of key/value pairs, which makes the model multi-dimensional.
notes.explanation: You can then filter and aggregate by any label, such as all requests with `status="500"`.

notes.front: What is PromQL?
notes.back: Prometheus’s flexible query language, built to make use of its multi-dimensional data.
notes.explanation: For example, a PromQL query over kube-state-metrics data can count the Pods that are not ready.

notes.front: How does Prometheus normally collect time series?
notes.back: By pulling: it scrapes its targets over HTTP.
notes.explanation: Each target exposes its current values at an endpoint, such as a Kubernetes component’s `/metrics`.

notes.front: How can time series be pushed to Prometheus, and for what?
notes.back: Through an intermediary push gateway, which supports short-lived jobs.
notes.explanation: Prometheus then scrapes the push gateway as usual, so the model stays pull-based.

notes.front: How does Prometheus find the targets it scrapes?
notes.back: Through service discovery or static configuration.
notes.explanation: Static configuration lists fixed targets; service discovery finds them automatically.

notes.front: Does a Prometheus server rely on distributed storage?
notes.back: No: each server is autonomous, so you can rely on it when other parts of your infrastructure are broken.
notes.explanation: Prometheus is designed to be the system you turn to during an outage.

notes.front: In the Prometheus ecosystem, what does the Prometheus server do?
notes.back: Scrapes and stores time series data, and runs rules over it to record new series or generate alerts.
notes.explanation: The other components, such as client libraries, exporters and Alertmanager, feed it or act on its output.

notes.front: What are Prometheus client libraries for?
notes.back: Instrumenting application code, so the application exposes its own metrics.
notes.explanation: They also provide the metric types, such as counters and gauges.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus exporter?
notes.back: A special-purpose component that exposes metrics for a service, such as HAProxy, StatsD or Graphite.
notes.explanation: Exporters let Prometheus monitor software you can’t instrument yourself.

notes.front: Which Prometheus component handles alerts?
notes.back: Alertmanager.
notes.explanation: The Prometheus server generates alerts from its rules; Alertmanager handles them from there.

notes.front: Which tool does the Prometheus overview name for visualising collected data?
notes.back: Grafana, or other API consumers.
notes.explanation: Prometheus stores and queries the data; Grafana draws the dashboards.

notes.front: When is Prometheus a poor choice?
notes.back: When you need 100% accuracy, such as for per-request billing: its data won’t be detailed and complete enough.
notes.explanation: It values reliability over completeness; use another system for billing and Prometheus for the rest.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, “Overview”, “When does it not fit?”

notes.front: Where and when did Prometheus start?
notes.back: At SoundCloud, in 2012.
notes.explanation: It is now a standalone open-source project, maintained independently of any company.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus counter?
notes.back: A cumulative metric whose value can only increase, or be reset to zero on restart.
notes.explanation: Never use a counter for a value that can fall, such as the number of running processes.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus gauge?
notes.back: A single numerical value that can go up and down arbitrarily.
notes.explanation: Typical gauges are temperatures, current memory usage and the number of concurrent requests.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus histogram?
notes.back: A metric that counts observations, such as request durations, into ranges you choose (buckets), and also records their sum.
notes.explanation: It is essentially a bucketed counter; quantiles, such as the 95th-percentile request time, can be calculated from it with `histogram_quantile()`, even across aggregated histograms.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus summary?
notes.back: Like a histogram, it samples observations with a count and sum, but it calculates configurable quantiles over a sliding time window.
notes.explanation: It exposes one series per quantile, e.g. quantile="0.95", plus `_sum` and `_count` series.

notes.front: Is OpenTelemetry an observability backend?
notes.back: No. Storing and visualising telemetry is deliberately left to other tools, such as Jaeger or Prometheus.
notes.explanation: OpenTelemetry generates, exports and collects telemetry and works with many backends, open-source and commercial.

notes.front: Which two principles does OpenTelemetry follow?
notes.back: You own the data you generate, with no vendor lock-in; and you learn only one set of APIs and conventions.
notes.explanation: Together they give teams the freedom to change backends without re-instrumenting.

notes.front: OpenTelemetry supports the three pillars as signals. Which fourth signal does it currently support?
notes.back: Baggage: contextual information passed between signals.
notes.explanation: Traces, metrics, logs and baggage are the four signals OpenTelemetry currently supports.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · OpenTelemetry docs as of that date

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry signals are still under development or at the proposal stage?
notes.back: Events, a specific type of log, and profiles, which record resource usage at the code level.
notes.explanation: They are not yet among the supported signals, so check the current docs before relying on them.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · OpenTelemetry docs as of that date

notes.front: What do Thanos and Cortex add to Prometheus?
notes.back: Distributed time series storage for multi-cluster or multi-cloud visibility: long-term storage (Cortex) and global querying (Thanos).
notes.explanation: Grafana Mimir is another Prometheus-compatible, horizontally scalable store.

notes.front: Your team needs a system that scrapes metrics from the Kubernetes components, stores them as time series and raises alerts. Which project fits?
notes.back: Prometheus.
notes.choices:
A) Prometheus
B) OpenTelemetry on its own
C) kube-state-metrics on its own
notes.choicesExplained: B: OpenTelemetry is not a backend; it doesn’t store or alert. C: kube-state-metrics only exposes object-state metrics for something like Prometheus to scrape.
notes.explanation: Prometheus is a monitoring and alerting toolkit, and Kubernetes components already expose metrics in its format.

notes.front: You want Prometheus to collect the kube-scheduler’s own metrics. Where does it scrape them?
notes.back: From the kube-scheduler’s `/metrics` endpoint, which serves them in Prometheus format.
notes.explanation: Every control plane component, and the kubelet and kube-proxy, exposes `/metrics` the same way.

notes.front: You want the kube-apiserver’s trace spans sampled and redacted before they reach Jaeger. What do you put in between, and which protocol feeds it?
notes.back: An OpenTelemetry Collector, receiving the spans over OTLP.
notes.explanation: The Collector receives spans, processes them, for example by sampling or redaction, and forwards them to a tracing backend.

notes.front: A request ID is attached to a request as it passes between services, so that its traces, metrics and logs can all carry it. Which OpenTelemetry signal is this?
notes.back: Baggage.
notes.explanation: Baggage is contextual information passed between signals.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · OpenTelemetry docs as of that date

notes.front: You want to track the total number of HTTP requests your service has served since it started. Which Prometheus metric type?
notes.back: A counter.
notes.choices:
A) Counter
B) Gauge
C) Summary
notes.choicesExplained: B: a gauge is for values that go up and down. C: a summary samples observations such as durations, not a running total.
notes.explanation: The total only goes up (or resets to zero on restart), which is exactly a counter.

notes.front: You want to track how many requests your service is handling right now. Which Prometheus metric type?
notes.back: A gauge.
notes.choices:
A) Counter
B) Gauge
C) Histogram
notes.choicesExplained: A: a counter can’t go down. C: a histogram buckets observations such as durations; it doesn’t hold a current level.
notes.explanation: The number of concurrent requests rises and falls, so it needs a type that can go down.

notes.front: You want to record request durations in buckets you choose, and later compute quantiles across many instances with `histogram_quantile()`. Which metric type?
notes.back: A histogram.
notes.choices:
A) Gauge
B) Histogram
C) Counter
notes.choicesExplained: A: a gauge holds one current value, not a distribution. C: a plain counter gives a total, with no buckets.
notes.explanation: `histogram_quantile()` works on histograms and on aggregations of histograms.

notes.front: You want the client itself to calculate configurable quantiles of response sizes over a sliding time window. Which metric type?
notes.back: A summary.
notes.explanation: A summary computes its quantiles over a sliding window and also gives a count and sum.

notes.front: A nightly batch job runs for 30 seconds, then exits. How do its metrics reach Prometheus?
notes.back: The job pushes them to a push gateway, which Prometheus then scrapes.
notes.choices:
A) Prometheus scrapes the job directly
B) The job pushes to a push gateway
C) Alertmanager forwards them
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pull model scrapes running targets; for short-lived jobs Prometheus provides the push gateway. C: Alertmanager handles alerts, not metric collection.
notes.explanation: The push gateway exists to support short-lived jobs.

notes.front: You want Prometheus to monitor an HAProxy load balancer whose code you can’t change. What do you use?
notes.back: An exporter for HAProxy.
notes.choices:
A) A client library
B) An exporter
C) Alertmanager
notes.choicesExplained: A: client libraries instrument code you can change. C: Alertmanager handles alerts; it does not produce metrics.
notes.explanation: Exporters expose metrics for services that aren’t instrumented themselves.

notes.front: You want to alert when Pods have been stuck `Terminating` for more than five minutes. Which add-on supplies the metric?
notes.back: kube-state-metrics.
notes.choices:
A) Metrics Server
B) kube-state-metrics
C) cAdvisor
notes.choicesExplained: A: Metrics Server gives only CPU and memory usage. C: cAdvisor reports container resource use, not object state.
notes.explanation: It exposes object state, such as deletion timestamps and status reasons, which Prometheus can alert on.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Metrics for Kubernetes Object States”

notes.front: A record shows one request spending 300 ms in the auth service and 20 ms in the database. Which pillar of observability is this?
notes.back: A trace.
notes.explanation: Traces link the timing and relationships of operations along one request’s path.

notes.front: “2026-09-25T10:02:11Z ERROR payment declined: card expired”. Which pillar of observability is this?
notes.back: A log.
notes.explanation: Logs are a chronological record of events, usually as timestamped text.

notes.front: `http_requests_total{status="500"} = 17`, recorded every 15 seconds. Which pillar of observability is this?
notes.back: A metric.
notes.explanation: Metrics are numerical measurements recorded over time, identified by a name and labels.

notes.front: Which cluster-level logging architecture does this diagram show?
notes.back: A node-level logging agent: one agent Pod per node reads every container’s log files and forwards them to the backend.
notes.explanation: The app writes to stdout and stderr as normal; the agent needs no change to the app.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Logging Architecture”, “Using a node logging agent”

image.alt: Diagram: my-pod’s app-container writes stdout and stderr to log-file.log on the node, which logrotate rotates; a separate logging-agent-pod with a logging-agent reads that file and exchanges data with a logging backend.

notes.front: Which cluster-level logging architecture does this diagram show?
notes.back: A streaming sidecar: a second container in the Pod re-emits the app’s logs on its own stdout and stderr, and the node agent collects them.
notes.explanation: The node’s kubelet and logging agent then handle the logs as usual, so `kubectl logs` still works.

image.alt: Diagram: inside my-pod, an app-container talks to a streaming container; the streaming container writes stdout and stderr to log-file.log on the node, rotated by logrotate; a separate logging-agent-pod reads the file and sends it to a logging backend.

notes.front: Which cluster-level logging architecture does this diagram show?
notes.back: A sidecar container running its own logging agent, which sends the app’s logs straight to the backend.
notes.explanation: Flexible, but costly in resources, and `kubectl logs` can’t see these logs.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Logging Architecture”, “Sidecar container with a logging agent”

image.alt: Diagram: inside my-pod, an app-container exchanges data with a logging-agent container in the same Pod, and that logging-agent exchanges data directly with a logging backend. No node log file is involved.

notes.front: Which cluster-level logging architecture does this diagram show?
notes.back: The application exposes or pushes its logs directly to the backend.
notes.explanation: The Kubernetes docs note that this is outside the scope of Kubernetes.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Logging Architecture”, “Exposing logs directly from the application”

image.alt: Diagram: inside my-pod, a single app-container exchanges data directly with a logging backend. There is no sidecar, no node log file and no logging agent.

notes.front: Your apps write to stdout. You want every node’s container logs in one central store, without changing the apps. Which approach does the Kubernetes documentation suggest?
notes.back: A node-level logging agent, run as a DaemonSet so there is one on every node.
notes.choices:
A) A logging-agent sidecar in every Pod
B) A node-level agent run as a DaemonSet
C) Change each app to push logs to the store
notes.choicesExplained: A: works, but costs resources in every Pod and hides logs from `kubectl logs`. C: this requires changing the apps, which you want to avoid.
notes.explanation: Node-level logging needs only one agent per node and no changes to the applications.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Logging Architecture”, “Using a node logging agent”

notes.front: A team instruments its services with OpenTelemetry and runs the OpenTelemetry Collector. Where can it search its traces?
notes.back: Nowhere yet: it still needs a tracing backend, such as Jaeger, because OpenTelemetry does not store telemetry.
notes.explanation: OpenTelemetry generates, collects and exports telemetry; storage and visualisation are left to other tools.

notes.front: Prometheus counter versus gauge: which can go down?
notes.back: Only a gauge. A counter only increases, apart from a reset to zero on restart.
notes.explanation: If a value can fall, such as running processes, use a gauge.

notes.front: Prometheus histogram versus summary: what is the difference?
notes.back: Both count and sum observations; a histogram puts them in buckets, while a summary calculates quantiles itself over a sliding window.
notes.explanation: Quantiles are computed from histograms later, with `histogram_quantile()`, even across aggregated histograms.

notes.front: The Metrics API versus a Prometheus pipeline: why isn’t the Metrics API enough for monitoring?
notes.back: It deliberately provides only the CPU and memory metrics needed for autoscaling and basic inspection; it doesn’t replace a full monitoring pipeline.
notes.explanation: For a more complete set of metrics, the docs suggest deploying a second, fuller metrics pipeline alongside it.

notes.front: Prometheus versus OpenTelemetry: what is the difference in role?
notes.back: Prometheus scrapes, stores and queries metrics; OpenTelemetry generates, collects and exports telemetry but is not a backend.
notes.explanation: They work together: OpenTelemetry can send data to backends such as Prometheus.

notes.front: Streaming sidecar versus sidecar with a logging agent: which keeps `kubectl logs` working?
notes.back: The streaming sidecar, which writes to stdout. A sidecar agent ships logs itself, so `kubectl logs` can’t see them.
notes.explanation: The sidecar agent is more flexible but also uses significant resources.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Logging Architecture”, “Sidecar container with a logging agent”

notes.front: kube-state-metrics versus Metrics Server: what does each report?
notes.back: kube-state-metrics reports object state, such as a Pod’s phase; Metrics Server reports CPU and memory usage.
notes.explanation: One tells you what Kubernetes thinks of an object; the other how much it is consuming.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Metrics for Kubernetes Object States”
